app.carbonExplainer.directEmissionsDesc: Trazo counts the emissions this operation causes directly — fuel, electricity, irrigation, equipment — plus the manufacturing of the fertilizer and crop-protection products it buys. It is not a full life-cycle assessment: transport to the farm, packaging, equipment manufacturing, distribution and end-of-life are all excluded.
app.carbonExplainer.directEmissionsUnit: kg of greenhouse gases (as CO2 equivalent) from recorded farm work and purchased inputs
app.carbonExplainer.disclaimer: Carbon calculations cover this operation's own fuel, electricity, irrigation and equipment use, plus the manufacturing of the fertilizer and crop-protection products it buys. They exclude transport to the farm, packaging, distribution, retail and end-of-life. Factor sources differ by input: fuel and electricity are EPA-published, nitrogen combines EPA and IPCC guideline values, crop-protection manufacturing comes from peer-reviewed LCA literature, and the phosphorus and potassium figures are Trazo's own conservative estimates where published values are sparse. Trazo is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or certified by the EPA or USDA.
app.carbonExplainer.epaDesc: Fuel combustion emissions use published EPA factors: diesel releases 10.21 kg CO2e per gallon, gasoline releases 8.78 kg CO2e per gallon. Grid electricity emissions are based on EPA eGRID 2023 regional averages.
app.carbonExplainer.epaUsdaNote: Factor sources differ by input — each one is shown with its own source, and some are Trazo estimates rather than agency figures.
app.carbonExplainer.fertilizerDesc: Crop nutrient production and field application
app.carbonExplainer.howWeCalculateDesc: We measure what happens on the farm, plus the manufacturing of the inputs it purchases. Transport, packaging, distribution and retail are excluded.
app.carbonExplainer.ipccDesc: When limestone (CaCO3) or dolomite is applied to soil for pH correction, CO2 is released through chemical dissolution. We use IPCC Tier 1 emission factors: limestone releases 0.44 kg CO2/kg, dolomite releases 0.477 kg CO2/kg.

app.carbonExplainer.scopeBoundary: Estimated emissions from the recorded activities included in this calculation. Missing activity data and excluded sources are not represented. Not a full life-cycle footprint: transport to the farm, packaging, equipment manufacturing and retail are excluded. Fuel and electricity factors are EPA-published; phosphorus and potassium are Trazo estimates where published values are sparse. Each factor shows its own source.
app.carbonExplainer.scopeBoundaryLime: Where carbonate-lime applications are recorded with their amount, their estimated CO₂ is included, using IPCC Tier 1 factors and assigned to the application year; this is not a measured release on the application date.

carbonPreview.noEmissions.pollinationTit: A biological service with no emissions
carbonPreview.noEmissions.pollination: Pollination is a biological service: no fuel burned, so there are no emissions to estimate. Hive counts and placement dates evidence the § 205.200 biodiversity practices your OSP describes.
carbonPreview.noEmissions.scouting: Scouting is observational, so there are no emissions to estimate. It is also the record § 205.206(e) rests on: a National List substance is permitted only where prevention proved insufficient.
carbonPreview.noEmissions.ipm: Biological control and beneficial releases have no emissions to estimate. They are the § 205.206(a)–(d) practices a certifier expects to see tried before any substance is applied.
carbonPreview.noEmissions.business: Certifications, inspections and audits have no emissions to estimate. Their dates and certificate numbers are what your certifier asks for at renewal.
carbonPreview.noEmissions.general: General farm work has no emissions to estimate. It still belongs in the record: § 205.103(b)(1) asks for records adapted to the particular business you run.
carbonPreview.noEmissions.weather: Weather has no emissions to estimate. It explains the gaps in a season when your certifier reads back through the record.

carbonPreview.note.organic_pesticide: Organic pesticide (neem, pyrethrin): a lower emission factor than synthetic pesticides.
carbonPreview.note.biological_pesticide: Biological pesticide (Bt, spinosad): a lower emission factor, because it is made by fermentation.
carbonPreview.note.organic_herbicide: Organic herbicide (acetic acid, vinegar): a lower emission factor than synthetic herbicides.
carbonPreview.note.copper_fungicide: Copper fungicide: a higher emission factor, for the energy used to mine and refine copper.
carbonPreview.note.sulfur_fungicide: Sulfur fungicide: a lower emission factor, as sulfur is often a by-product of oil and gas refining.
carbonPreview.note.biological_fungicide: Biological fungicide (Bacillus, Trichoderma): a lower emission factor, because it is made by fermentation.
carbonPreview.note.organic_fungicide: Organic fungicide (neem oil, potassium bicarbonate): a lower emission factor, from natural extraction.
carbonPreview.note.organic_fertilizer: Organic fertilizer: little manufacturing or processing, plus the field N₂O from the nitrogen applied (IPCC 2019, direct and indirect). Field N₂O depends on the nitrogen, not on how it was made.
carbonPreview.note.slow_release_fertiliz: Slow-release fertilizer: the factor includes a 10% premium for the coating.

consumer.education.pageDescription: Understand how QR pages and farm documentation help you make informed food choices
consumer.education.topic1.description: Learn what a farm's documented practices tell you, and what they don't
consumer.education.topic1.section1.body: Each product page lists the farming activities the producer recorded during the season — planting, irrigation, soil work, pest management, harvest — with the date each one happened. Where a photo was taken, you can see it. These are the farmer's own records, shown to you as they were entered.
consumer.education.topic1.section2.body: Trazo does not verify farming practices and does not certify anyone. When a farm is listed as certified organic, that status comes from its certifier and is cross-referenced against the USDA Organic Integrity Database. Everything else on the page is the producer's own account of their season.
consumer.education.topic1.section3.body: Trazo asks producers to log activities as the season happens rather than reconstruct them later. A page with more entries means the farm kept a fuller record — not that its food is better. Read the practices themselves and decide what matters to you.
consumer.education.topic1.section3.headi: Why the record gets fuller over time
consumer.education.topic1.tip: A longer record means more of the season was written down. It is a measure of documentation, not of quality — the practices listed are what tell you how the food was grown.
consumer.education.topic1.title: What the farm record shows you
consumer.education.topic2.description: A quick guide to everything you see when you scan a Trazo QR code on a product
consumer.education.topic2.section1.body: The top of a QR page names the product, the farm that grew it, and when the season ran. Below that is the timeline: the farming activities the producer recorded, in the order they happened, with photos where they took them. There is no overall grade — the practices themselves are what you read.
consumer.education.topic2.section1.headi: What is at the top of the page
consumer.education.topic2.section2.body: Below the header you will find a timeline of farming events. Each card represents an activity the farmer documented: planting, irrigation, soil management, chemical applications, harvest, and more. Cards with photos show what was done. Tap any event to see its full details.
consumer.education.topic2.section3.body: Badges appear beside the record. A certification shown as 'Verified' means Trazo confirmed the farm's own entry in the USDA Organic Integrity Database, a public register of certified operations. Certifications without a confirmed entry, including a similar name that was not confirmed, are labeled 'Self-Reported': the farm entered them, and they have not been independently checked. Carbon figures, where shown, are estimates from the farm's recorded fuel, energy and purchased inputs, and the card says what each estimate is based on.
consumer.education.topic2.tip: Scroll down past the timeline to see the farm's story, location information, and environmental impact details in expandable sections.
consumer.education.topic2.title: How to Read a QR Page
consumer.education.topic3.description: How documented farming practices build trust and why transparent farms deserve your support
consumer.education.topic3.section1.body: Most food labels are self-declared, and a shopper has no way to look behind them. Trazo does not resolve that by adding another label — it publishes the underlying record instead: what was applied, when, by which practice, with the farm's certification shown as its certifier issued it. You judge the practices yourself.
consumer.education.topic3.section2.body: Traditional carbon platforms have a perverse incentive: farms that log fewer activities appear to have lower emissions, rewarding them for hiding practices. Trazo works the other way — the more a farm documents, the more of its season you can read. Farms are rewarded for showing you everything.
consumer.education.topic3.section3.body: Every time you scan a QR code, you are supporting a farmer who chose to be transparent about their practices. Your engagement tells producers that consumers value openness, which encourages more farms to document and share their growing journey.
consumer.education.topic3.tip: You are supporting farmers who choose openness over secrecy. Every scan and review reinforces the value of agricultural transparency.
consumer.education.topic3.title: Why Farm Transparency Matters
consumer.education.topic4.description: How your feedback helps other consumers and motivates farms to keep improving
consumer.education.topic4.section1.body: After scanning any QR code, you can leave a quick comment at the bottom of the product page without creating an account. This anonymous feedback helps farms understand what consumers care about and what questions they have.
consumer.education.topic4.section2.body: Create a free account to leave detailed reviews with star ratings and photos. Your review appears on the QR page for future scanners, helping other consumers make informed choices. You can rate the product, share your experience, and upload photos of how you used it.
consumer.education.topic4.section3.body: Your reviews create a feedback loop: consumers share experiences, farms learn what matters to buyers, and everyone benefits from more transparency. Farms that document thoroughly give you the most to go on.
consumer.education.topic4.tip: Your review is visible to every person who scans that product's QR code. A thoughtful review can help hundreds of future consumers.
consumer.education.topic4.title: Leaving Reviews and Building Community

consumer.eventCard.organic.tooltipOmri: This record is matched to an entry on OMRI's Products List in Trazo's catalog. OMRI reviews materials, not farms: the match does not show that this application was approved or met the listing's restrictions.
consumer.eventCard.organic.tooltipWsda: This product name is matched to the Washington State Department of Agriculture (WSDA) Materials List in Trazo's catalog. WSDA runs a state programme that registers inputs for use in organic production, and many certifiers accept it in place of an OMRI listing. education.detail.bufferZones.adjoiningUs: What's on the other side of the line — a conventional orchard, a road, a residential lot.
education.detail.bufferZones.bufferType: The physical barrier — hedgerow, ditch, access road — and its width in feet.
education.detail.bufferZones.disposition: Crop grown inside the buffer row can never be sold as organic. Record its disposition — not harvested, left in the field, sold as conventional, and so on.
What happens to anything grown in the buffer row:
education.detail.bufferZones.driftDesc: 7 CFR 205.400(f)(1) requires you to notify your certifying agent, in writing, of any drift that could affect your organic status. Keep the notification and any response on file alongside your buffer records.
education.detail.bufferZones.driftTitle: If a neighbor's application drifts onto your land
education.detail.bufferZones.lastProhibi: This is what actually decides whether a border needs a buffer at all — no recent prohibited-material use next door, no buffer required.
Date the neighboring land last received a prohibited material:
education.detail.bufferZones.recordPerBo: What to record at every border
education.detail.bufferZones.ruleDesc: 7 CFR 205.202(c) requires your certified land to have distinct boundaries and buffer zones sufficient to prevent contact with prohibited substances applied on adjoining land. A buffer isn't automatic everywhere — it depends on what's happening next door.
education.detail.bufferZones.whereDesc: Add each border in the Parcel Application's buffer editor. At harvest, the buffer-row disposition field on the harvest form captures what happened to that strip's crop for the season.
education.detail.bufferZones.whereTitle: Where to record it in Trazo
education.detail.carbonData.b2b3: Emissions data for sustainability assessments: the operation's own, plus the manufacturing of the inputs it buys
education.detail.carbonData.bestOfBothDe: Trazo maintains full calculation accuracy for business reporting while the consumer page stays in plain words: documented practices and photos first, environmental data available on request. Shoppers never see a grade.
education.detail.carbonData.consumerFocu: "See how this was grown" — the documented practices, in plain words
education.detail.carbonData.contextDesc: Trazo started carbon-first and moved away from it, because leading with carbon penalizes the farm that documents more: every additional logged pass adds emissions and makes the number look worse. Recordkeeping does the opposite — the more you log, the stronger your file. Carbon is still calculated from the same activities, in the background, for the buyers who ask for it.
education.detail.carbonData.expandable: Full carbon data available for interested consumers
education.detail.carbonData.internal4: Year-on-year comparison of your own operation
education.detail.carbonData.primaryMetri: Documented practices — the record itself is what certifiers review and buyers check
education.detail.carbonData.realFarm: Calculations based on actual fuel, fertilizer, and equipment use
education.detail.carbonData.scope: Focus on farmer-controlled emissions (direct operations only)
education.detail.carbonData.secondary: Environmental data — available for interested consumers and B2B reporting
education.detail.carbonData.trustBuild: Focus on documented practices over numerical accuracy
education.detail.carbonData.updates: Factors are reviewed against current publications (EPA eGRID 2023, EPA 40 CFR Part 98, IPCC 2019)
education.detail.carbonData.usdaVerified: Each factor names its source: the EPA for fuel, electricity and nitrogen, academic studies for pesticides, and Trazo estimates for phosphorus and potassium
education.detail.carbonMethodology.calcS: When you log an activity, we capture fuel used, area covered, chemicals applied, and equipment hours.
We apply the emission factor for that input, from the source listed for it on this page.
All values are converted to kg CO₂e (carbon dioxide equivalent) for consistent comparison.
Input total = manufacturing emissions + application fuel emissions
education.detail.carbonMethodology.chemi: Sources: Lal (2004) and Audsley et al. for pesticide/herbicide manufacturing LCA, International Copper Association LCA Studies, EPA Industrial Manufacturing for sulfur byproduct factors
education.detail.carbonMethodology.conti: Factors are checked against the latest publications. Last full review: December 2025 (EPA eGRID2023, 40 CFR Part 98, IPCC 2019). Updates are applied when a source publishes new data.
education.detail.carbonMethodology.diese: Confidence Level: 95% - This is the most reliable emission factor as it comes directly from federal regulatory standards.
EPA Mobile Combustion Factor: 10.21 kg CO₂ per gallon of diesel
Source: EPA Greenhouse Gas Emission Factors Hub (40 CFR Part 98) - Mobile combustion for agricultural equipment
Other field work: 2.5 gallons per hectare
education.detail.carbonMethodology.direc: Trazo estimates the operation's own emissions plus the manufacturing of the fertilizer and chemicals it buys: fuel burned, electricity used, and the inputs applied. It is not a full life-cycle assessment: transport to the farm, packaging and equipment manufacturing are left out.
education.detail.carbonMethodology.eiaDe: U.S. Energy Information Administration - electricity generation and emissions data validation (0.81 lbs/kWh = 0.367 kg/kWh for 2023).
education.detail.carbonMethodology.elect: Irrigation pumps (deep well 200+ ft): 3.5 kWh per 1,000 gallons pumped
Irrigation pumps (standard 50-100 ft): 0.85 kWh per 1,000 gallons pumped
Wind machines (frost protection): 35 kWh per hour
Misting systems: 12 kWh per hour per acre
Confidence Level: 95% - Based on the national electricity grid mix; actual emissions vary by region.
EPA eGRID U.S. Average: 0.365 kg CO₂e per kWh (delivered electricity)
Source: EPA eGRID2023 Summary Tables rev.2 (U.S. 770.9 lb CO₂e/MWh) adjusted for 4.2% grid gross loss
education.detail.carbonMethodology.epaEg: U.S. average electricity emission factors (770.9 lbs CO₂e/MWh for 2023). Accounts for the mix of energy sources in the electrical grid.
education.detail.carbonMethodology.epaGh: 40 CFR Part 98 - The official U.S. Environmental Protection Agency source for stationary and mobile combustion emission factors. Updated annually.
EPA Greenhouse Gas Emission Factors Hub
education.detail.carbonMethodology.examp: Applying 100 liters of synthetic herbicide over 5 hectares:
Manufacturing: 100L × 1.0 kg/L × 4.1% AI × 5.5 kg CO₂/kg = 22.55 kg CO₂e
Application fuel: 5 ha × 0.8 L diesel/ha ÷ 3.79 × 10.21 kg/gal = 10.8 kg CO₂e
education.detail.carbonMethodology.ferti: Nitrogen source: EPA 40 CFR Part 98 (manufacturing) + IPCC 2006/2019 Guidelines (N₂O: EF1 = 1% of applied N × 44/28 × GWP 265). Phosphorus and potassium: Trazo conservative estimates.
education.detail.carbonMethodology.ipccD: Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change - N₂O emission factors for agricultural soils (EF1 = 1% of applied N, GWP = 265).
education.detail.carbonMethodology.organ: Organic fertilizers (compost, manure) have much lower emissions: only 0.5 kg CO₂/kg due to minimal manufacturing process.
education.detail.carbonMethodology.pesti: Lal (2004): Herbicides 6.3±2.7, Insecticides 5.1±3.0, Fungicides 3.9±2.2 kg CO₂e/kg AI. Audsley et al.: Higher estimates (18-27 kg for herbicides).
education.detail.carbonMethodology.usdaA: Farm energy use data, fuel use in crop work, and agricultural machinery efficiency standards.
education.detail.carbonMethodology.usdaN: National Engineering Handbook Chapter 8 - Energy consumption factors for irrigation pumping systems based on depth, volume, and equipment efficiency.
USDA NRCS Irrigation Pumping Plants Guide
education.detail.carbonMethodology.verif: Each emission factor names its source, and the sources differ by input. Fuel and electricity factors come from the EPA; nitrogen from the EPA and the IPCC guidelines; pesticides and herbicides from published academic life-cycle studies. Phosphorus and potassium are Trazo's own conservative estimates, and are labelled that way. Each source is listed below.
education.detail.consumerEngagement.edu: QR pages become teaching moments about sustainable farming
education.detail.consumerEngagement.geog: The approximate region a scan came from, derived from a hashed IP — never a person, never an address
education.detail.consumerEngagement.intr: Finishing a season gives you one link that shows what you did, in plain words, with photos and dates. It is for the wholesale buyer doing diligence before a commitment, and for the shopper holding the package. This covers where to put it and what the scan data can honestly tell you.
education.detail.consumerEngagement.mark: Website Integration: Embed your buyer-page link on product pages
Buyer follow-up: send the link with your spec sheet or after a sample ships
Email Marketing: Include QR codes in newsletters and customer communications
Retail partners: give the buyer a link they can check before they list you
Scan patterns: where and when interest shows up is a useful signal about which markets are checking your story — the counts are directional, never a customer list
education.detail.consumerEngagement.metr: Trazo counts scans; it does not know how many units you shipped, how far anyone scrolled, or how long they stayed. Treat the numbers as a sign of interest, not a conversion rate — and be wary of anyone selling you one.
education.detail.consumerEngagement.mobi: Readable one-handed on a phone, which is where most scans happen
education.detail.consumerEngagement.pack: "Scan to see how this was grown"
Minimum 1 inch square for easy scanning
Scan from 3 feet to ensure readability
education.detail.consumerEngagement.pos1: Table signs with your QR code and farm story
education.detail.consumerEngagement.pos2: Shelf talkers linking to your documented growing record
education.detail.consumerEngagement.pos3: Product page QR codes for digital purchases
education.detail.consumerEngagement.pos4: A printed code at the farm store or stand, next to the price
education.detail.consumerEngagement.prem: A complete, checkable record gives a buyer something to verify before they commit
education.detail.consumerEngagement.repe: Consumers return to farmers they trust and understand
education.detail.consumerEngagement.retu: Repeat visits — someone coming back to check your latest season
education.detail.consumerEngagement.tota: How many times the page was opened, with duplicate scans from the same device counted separately
education.detail.consumerEngagement.trus: A buyer who can check the record does not have to take your word for it
education.detail.consumerEngagement.wom: Consumers are more likely to recommend farms whose practices they can see and trust
education.detail.eventMastery.autoTransc: A voice note pre-fills part of the form — review it and complete the rest
education.detail.eventMastery.batch1: Log several activities at the end of the day
education.detail.eventMastery.batch3: Use farm notes to remember details
education.detail.eventMastery.batch4: Still counts toward your season's record
education.detail.eventMastery.handsFree: Speak your notes quickly, then review the pre-filled fields later
education.detail.eventMastery.intro: How to build a season record your certifier can review without follow-up questions: when to log, what to photograph, and what to skip.
education.detail.eventMastery.photo1: Equipment in action (tractors, harvesters, irrigation systems)
education.detail.eventMastery.photo2: Product application (fertilizers, organic amendments, pest treatments)
education.detail.eventMastery.photo4: Quality indicators (soil conditions, plant health, weather conditions)
education.detail.eventMastery.quickNotes: Perfect for recording observations while working
education.detail.eventMastery.realTime1: Log activities as they happen in the field
education.detail.eventMastery.realTime2: Log from your phone's browser in the field — photos upload straight from the camera
education.detail.eventMastery.realTime3: Voice recording feature for quick notes
education.detail.eventMastery.realTime4: Captures details while they're fresh and accurate
education.detail.eventMastery.successDes: Log every activity you actually perform, and photograph the ones an inspector will want to see: planting, harvest and any material you apply. A season is complete when it answers its own questions — not when it reaches a number.
education.detail.eventMastery.successTit: What a Complete Season Looks Like
education.detail.eventMastery.tip1: Use good lighting - avoid shadows on equipment/crops
education.detail.eventMastery.tip2: Include context - show the broader field/operation
education.detail.eventMastery.tip4: Include measurement tools for scale reference
education.detail.eventMastery.voiceComma: "Record fertilizer application, 50 pounds organic compost, north field"
education.detail.farmEvents.bufferUseDes: Crop harvested off a buffer strip. It cannot be sold as organic under § 205.202(c), so it gets its own record and never counts toward the organic lot.
education.detail.farmEvents.businessDesc: Inspections, certificate renewals, certifier correspondence, training. Paperwork with a date on it.
education.detail.farmEvents.cleanoutDesc: Purging a bin, a sprayer or a line before organic product runs through it — the § 205.272 evidence that nothing was commingled.
education.detail.farmEvents.fieldWorkDes: Cultivation, mowing, thinning, bed prep — the passes you make through the crop.
education.detail.farmEvents.frostProtect: Wind machines, heaters or sprinklers on a cold night — hours run and fuel burned.
education.detail.farmEvents.harvestDesc: Each pick: quantity, unit and method. These are the records the season's lot header is built from, so log every pick, not just the last one.
education.detail.farmEvents.inputApplica: Any material applied to the crop — fertilizer, foliar feed, a pest or disease material. Trazo checks the product against your approved-inputs list and the National List as you save.
education.detail.farmEvents.intro: Every entry point in Trazo (the Activities page, Log activity on a parcel, the form's own chooser) opens the same question: what did you do? You answer with one of the activities in the picker, in the words a grower uses. You never pick a database category. Each one routes to the right record behind the scenes and asks only the fields that activity actually needs.
education.detail.farmEvents.irrigationDe: Water applied — method, depth or volume, and the source it came from.
education.detail.farmEvents.notSalesDesc: “Certification & compliance” has no sales field, and that is deliberate. A sale is a transaction against harvested product, not a dated practice on a parcel, and it carries a buyer name that does not belong on your public timeline. Record sales in Sales Records on the season page: that is what the packet's mass balance reads.
education.detail.farmEvents.otherDesc: The escape hatch. Anything real that none of the other activities describes; a note with a date beats no record.
education.detail.farmEvents.pestDesc: What you found and what you did about it — including the scouting rounds where you found nothing, which are what show a monitoring plan is real.
education.detail.farmEvents.plantingDesc: Seed or transplants going in: variety, source, treatment status, and whether the seed was organic.
education.detail.farmEvents.pollinationD: Hives placed or pulled: dates, how many colonies, and who supplied them.
education.detail.farmEvents.proTipDesc: The right question is “what did I do today”, not “which record type is this”. Pick the verb that matches the work; the form asks for the rest. An inspector traces a sold lot back through these records, so a thin week is a gap in the trace — but an invented record is much worse than a missing one.
education.detail.farmEvents.proTipTitle: Log the day, not the category
education.detail.farmEvents.pruningDesc: Winter pruning, summer hedging, leaf pulling, shoot positioning — one pass, one record.
education.detail.farmEvents.seedSearchDe: The documented attempts to source organic seed before falling back to untreated conventional. Its own record because it happens before planting, not during it.
education.detail.farmEvents.soilDesc: Compost, manure, lime, gypsum, cover-crop incorporation, and soil tests. Raw manure starts the 90/120-day pre-harvest clock, so the date matters.
education.detail.farmEvents.transportDes: A load leaving the farm: where it went and who took it. Logged on its own because a load usually ships days after the pick it belongs to.
education.detail.farmEvents.weatherDesc: Frost, hail, a heat run, strong wind: the conditions that explain a decision you made or a yield your certifier will ask about.
education.detail.firstProduction.addPhot: Take photos of your farming activities — they are the evidence an inspector asks for

Expected harvest window and quantity estimates
education.detail.firstProduction.qrCreat: A unique QR code is created when you finish the season: buyers scan it to see your documented practices. The same records feed your readiness checks and your Organic System Plan modules.
education.detail.firstProduction.quickSt: Document everything from day one! Even basic activities like soil preparation and seed planting build your season's record — and the earlier you start, the less there is to reconstruct at renewal time.
education.detail.firstProduction.readyDe: This guide walks you through starting your first season in Trazo and logging your first activities. Everything you log starts working twice: toward your certifier-ready records and Organic System Plan, and toward the page your buyer can scan.

education.detail.gettingStarted.benefit2: Give wholesale buyers a record they can check before they commit

One link, not a sales deck:
education.detail.gettingStarted.revoluti: Every activity you log builds two things at once: a certifier-ready compliance record (with the regulation citations attached) and a buyer-facing story (in plain words). You are never penalized for documenting more — a fuller record is a stronger file on both sides.
education.detail.gettingStarted.step1: Record each activity as it happens, choosing from the activities in the picker
education.detail.gettingStarted.step2: Trazo carries what it already knows into the OSP modules and parcel applications as suggestions — a small number of questions, and never saved until you accept them. The plan is in your words because the rule requires it to be
education.detail.gettingStarted.step2Lab: Your records feed it, you write it:
education.detail.gettingStarted.step3: When you finish a season, a scannable QR code is created for its lot
education.detail.gettingStarted.step4: Buyers and shoppers scan the QR code to see your documented practices, photos, and certifications
education.detail.gettingStarted.step5: A fuller record means fewer questions you cannot answer when a buyer or certifier asks
education.detail.gettingStarted.welcomeD: Trazo turns the work you already do into records that work twice: once for your certifier (modules, applications, renewal packet) and once for your buyer (a scannable page of documented practices). Log each activity as it happens — Trazo assembles the rest.
education.detail.gettingStarted.whyTrans: In USDA's 2021 Organic Survey (NASS), over half of organic farms named recordkeeping and paperwork among their top challenges. Buyers increasingly ask for documentation before they commit. Trazo's answer: log once, and let the same record serve your certifier and your buyer.
education.detail.inspectionPrep.equipmen: A cleaning log for equipment, harvest bins, storage, or the transport vehicle, dated between the conventional and organic use.
If this equipment, these bins, or this transport also touch conventional ground, how do you prevent commingling?
education.detail.inspectionPrep.handlerA: The facility recorded in the season's post-harvest section, with its address and current organic certificate. From the moment your crop leaves, the audit trail runs through their records, not yours. Record the certificate date: Trazo prints the status exactly as your record supports it (current, expired or older than 15 months, or no date on file) and will not call a certificate current when the date is missing. If the operation is not certified, describe the records they give you that keep the product's organic identity intact.
education.detail.inspectionPrep.handlerQ: Who hulls, packs, dries or stores this crop once it leaves — and is their organic certificate current?
education.detail.inspectionPrep.handlerT: Whoever handles your crop off the farm
education.detail.inspectionPrep.inputsAn: An input or soil activity logged with product, rate, date, area, applicator, and its National List status.
education.detail.inspectionPrep.inputsQu: Which product, at what rate, on what date, on which parcel, applied by whom — and is it approved for organic use?
education.detail.inspectionPrep.introDes: An organic inspection traces your operation from field to sale, checking that every input, seed source, and harvest lot matches your Organic System Plan. Trazo's readiness checks point at pieces that still need attention before the visit — they're a preparation aid, never a certification finding. Only your certifying agent makes that call.
education.detail.inspectionPrep.mapAnswe: A map attached to the parcel application. Trazo draws the boundary and labels adjoining land use from your buffer records, and it travels inside the packet — but your certifier also wants roads and landmarks, block identifiers, and the other areas of your operation, which a boundary drawing cannot show. Attach your own 8.5x11 map (satellite imagery preferred) in section E. CCOF reviews it before inspecting a new parcel; WSDA asks for one with every site application, with your operation and site name printed on the map itself.
education.detail.inspectionPrep.mapQuest: Can you show the boundary of this parcel, what borders it, and where your buffers sit?
education.detail.inspectionPrep.readines: Run your readiness checks a few weeks ahead of the visit so you have time to fill any gaps before your certifier's inspector arrives.
Before the visit, not during it
education.detail.inspectionPrep.retentio: 7 CFR 205.103(b)(4) requires you to keep records for at least 5 years, retrievable within a reasonable time of a request. That applies to every record above, not just the current season.
education.detail.inspectionPrep.seedAnsw: Under 7 CFR 205.204, organic seed comes first. When it isn't commercially available, most certifiers expect a documented search of at least three sources before you buy untreated non-organic seed — keep that search on file.
education.detail.inspectionPrep.seedQues: Did you use organic seed? If not, why wasn't it commercially available?
education.detail.inspectionPrep.tracebac: Harvest records with lot numbers, a storage location, and sales records that reconcile quantity in against quantity out (mass balance) at every step.
Can you connect a sold lot back to the parcel it came from, with the quantities matching at every step?
Trazo runs this walk on your records and names every missing link.
education.detail.organicSystemPlan.commo: USDA publishes a standard Common OSP template that most certifying agents now accept, organized into numbered modules covering topics like general operation info, land history, seed sourcing, and monitoring. Trazo's guided modules follow that same structure, so your answers map onto the document your certifier expects.
education.detail.organicSystemPlan.guide: Each module asks plain-language questions in English or Spanish — no legal drafting required.
education.detail.organicSystemPlan.howTr: How Trazo helps you fill it out
education.detail.organicSystemPlan.naAtt: If a module doesn't apply to your operation, attest Not Applicable instead of skipping it. A module marked reviewed-and-N/A tells your certifier it was considered — a module left blank does not.
education.detail.organicSystemPlan.packe: Download any module as a PDF, or generate the full renewal packet — cover page, the § 205.406 annual update, your change notices, module PDFs and each parcel's application — from the records you've already logged.
Module PDFs and a renewal packet:
education.detail.organicSystemPlan.planR: Trazo lists what your dated records did after each of your answers was written — new ground, seasons, notices, materials, affidavits, incidents, parcels the plan never names. A list to re-read against, never a verdict: it does not read your prose and it never blocks submission.
education.detail.organicSystemPlan.sugge: Where your logged activities already answer a question, Trazo shows a suggested answer. You confirm or edit every one: a suggestion is never saved on your behalf.
education.detail.organicSystemPlan.whatI: Under 7 CFR 205.201(a), you write your Organic System Plan describing your practices, inputs, and monitoring. Your certifying agent reviews and evaluates it — Trazo only helps you assemble it.
Your OSP is a producer document, written by you
education.detail.organicSystemPlan.where: Open Organic System Plan in the sidebar to start or continue your modules.
education.detail.ospData.authorDesc: Trazo does not draft your plan out of your activity log, and it should not. § 205.201(a) makes the producer the author — the words have to be yours, because you are the one certifying they are true. Your records do something different and just as valuable: they suggest an answer where the answer already sits in your data, and they stand behind the plan as evidence when the inspector traces it.
education.detail.ospData.authorTitle: You write the plan; your records prove it
education.detail.ospData.introDesc: § 205.201(a) says an organic system plan must describe six things. Trazo's modules ask you plain questions, then compile your answers into exactly those six sections — so the plan your certifier reads is organized the way the rule is written, not the way the software happens to store it.
education.detail.ospData.introTitle: Your plan has six required parts
education.detail.ospData.lockDesc: A submitted plan is a snapshot — it is the document your certifier is reviewing, so it stops taking edits. To change anything, start a new version. The new version copies every answer across, and the approved-inputs registry with it, while the submitted version stays on file exactly as the certifier saw it.
education.detail.ospData.parcelDesc: A farm-wide module cannot answer a field-specific question. Land history, buffers and adjoining land use are asked once per parcel in that parcel's own application, and each parcel's answers print in the packet under its own name. New ground means a new application, not an edit to an old one.
education.detail.ospData.prefillDesc: A handful of questions arrive with a suggestion drawn from what Trazo already knows — your parcels, your farm profile, the materials you have logged. A suggestion is never saved for you. It waits beside the field until you accept it or type something better. Most questions carry no suggestion at all, and that is honest: nothing in your data can answer “how do you prevent commingling at harvest”.
education.detail.ospData.registryDesc: Materials Application → “Your materials list” is where each fertilizer and each pest, disease or weed material goes on the plan, with its OMRI listing, WSDA registration or National List citation. Those entries live on the plan itself, not in your activity log, and they are what prints into the (a)(2) inputs list. Leave the panel empty and your packet reports that no approved-inputs list is on file — even if you have been logging those same materials all season.
education.detail.ospData.registryTitle: The approved-inputs registry is part of the plan
education.detail.ospData.section1: Practices and procedures — § 205.201(a)(1). How you actually farm: rotation, tillage, fertility, pest, disease and weed management.
education.detail.ospData.section2: Inputs and materials — § 205.201(a)(2). Every substance you apply, what is in it, and where it comes from.
education.detail.ospData.section3: Monitoring — § 205.201(a)(3). What you watch, how often, and what you do when a practice is not working.
education.detail.ospData.section4: Recordkeeping — § 205.201(a)(4). The records you keep, and how a sold lot is traced back through them.
education.detail.ospData.section5: Contact and commingling barriers — § 205.201(a)(5). What keeps prohibited substances and non-organic crop away from organic ground and organic product.
education.detail.ospData.section6: Anything else your certifier asks for — § 205.201(a)(6).
education.detail.ospData.updateDesc: § 205.400(f)(2) is about telling your certifier when something changes — a new field, a new material, a new handler — immediately, at the time it changes. (Its sibling, § 205.400(f)(1), is the separate duty to report a prohibited substance applied to or drifted onto your ground.) § 205.406 is the once-a-year renewal: a summary of what changed since the last update, plus anything the certifier asked you to correct. Trazo keeps them apart because your certifier does. Filing the annual update in October does not cover a change you should have reported in March. File a change notice from the Organic System Plan page — the Change notifications panel — and when a notice names a parcel, it prints on that parcel's application in the packet, next to the records it has to agree with.
education.detail.ospData.updateTitle: A change notice and an annual update are not the same thing
education.detail.ospData.whereDesc: Farm → Organic System Plan. Each module is a card carrying its own status; “Narrative view & lifecycle” shows the six compiled sections exactly as they will print, and “Download packet” builds the file you send.
education.detail.qrCodes.consumerLanguag: Documented practices and photos — never jargon, never a grade
education.detail.qrCodes.envDetails: Environmental data in an expandable section — never the headline
education.detail.qrCodes.farmStory: "See exactly how this avocado was grown"
education.detail.qrCodes.instantTrust: The documented practice timeline, with photos where they exist
education.detail.qrCodes.mobileFirst: Mobile-First Design: Pages load in under 1.5s on mobile devices
education.detail.qrCodes.placement: Strategic Placement: Product packaging, farmers market signs, website
education.detail.qrCodes.progressiveLoad: Documented practices load first (under 1.5s), then details
education.detail.qrCodes.successDesc: A QR page shows a shopper the practices behind the product and the farm's certification as its certifier issued it, rather than a label they have to take on faith.
education.detail.qrCodes.tracking: Track Performance: Monitor scan rates and consumer engagement
education.detail.qrCodes.trustBuilders: Real farmer photos, third-party certification status
education.detail.qrCodes.updates: Regular Updates: Fresh content keeps consumers engaged
education.detail.qrCodes.valueProp: Clear Value Proposition: "Scan to see how this was grown"
education.detail.recordCorrections.good1: File the correction as soon as you find the discrepancy. Most of them surface while you are assembling the renewal packet, and that is a perfectly normal time to file one.
education.detail.recordCorrections.good2: One correction per value, each with its own reason, rather than one vague note covering several.
education.detail.recordCorrections.good3: Point at the paperwork that settles it: the weigh ticket, the invoice, the bag tag, the lab report.
education.detail.recordCorrections.good4: Never open a second record to “balance” a wrong one. Two records describing one activity is the finding; a corrected record with a reason is not.
education.detail.recordCorrections.goodP: Correct it, don't work around it
education.detail.recordCorrections.hitLo: You are not doing anything wrong, and nothing is lost. Trazo shows a notice explaining that the season is filed, with the way forward attached — a “Correct this record” button on the record itself. Nothing is deleted or overwritten at any point.
What you see if you try to edit one
education.detail.recordCorrections.limit: A correction fixes a value on a record that exists. It cannot add an activity you never logged inside the closed season, and it cannot change the season header — the harvest amount, lot number, grade and method are frozen when you finish, so check those before you confirm. A finished season cannot be reopened. If a header figure turns out to be wrong, tell your certifier what happened and keep the weigh tickets or invoices that show the correct figure. Work dated after the finish date is different: a shipment from storage, cover crop, post-harvest field work — that is not a correction at all. Log it as a normal activity with its own later date.
education.detail.recordCorrections.lockD: While a season is open, edit anything freely: it is your working record. When you finish the season, Trazo closes it: its activities stop accepting ordinary edits, and the lot header (harvest amount, lot number, quality grade, harvest method) is frozen. This is deliberate. Under 7 CFR 205.103(b)(2) an inspector traces a sold lot back to the parcel it came from, and that trace is only worth anything if the records did not quietly move after the fact.
education.detail.recordCorrections.lockT: Finishing a season makes its records read-only
education.detail.recordCorrections.packe: The record shows the corrected value, and the original stays beside it. Your certifier packet carries a Documented Corrections table for the season listing, for each correction: the date you made it, which record and which field, what was originally recorded, what it was corrected to, your reason, and who made it. That table is a strength, not an admission — it is the difference between a record that was maintained and one that cannot be checked.
education.detail.recordCorrections.step1: On the season's activity timeline, every record in a finished season carries the button.
Open the record and choose Correct this record:
education.detail.recordCorrections.step2: Trazo offers the fields most often corrected first; “Show all fields on this record type” opens the rest. One correction fixes one value.
Pick the value that is wrong:
education.detail.recordCorrections.step3: The date, the lot number, the rate — whatever the paperwork in your hand actually says.
education.detail.recordCorrections.step4: The reason is required. Your inspector reads it: a correction with a reason answers a question, one without raises it. “Transcription error — the lot on the bag tag and the invoice is …-880, keyed as …-088” is exactly right.
Say why, in your own words:
education.detail.recordCorrections.where: Open the season from its parcel, find the record in the timeline, and use Correct this record. Records in a season that is still open are edited normally, no correction needed.
education.detail.renewalSeason.certifier: Every certifier sets its own calendar. These are typical dates — confirm yours directly with your certifying agent.
education.detail.renewalSeason.completeU: Any changes to your operation since last year — new fields, new inputs, new buyers
An updated input list with current labels and National List/OMRI/WSDA status
A full season of field, harvest and sales records tying back to your OSP
Your OCCSP cost-share application, if you're applying this year
What a complete annual update contains
education.detail.renewalSeason.migrating: If you're moving off a spreadsheet or another recordkeeping tool — including COG Pro, which has announced it is ending service December 31, 2026 — export everything before you lose access. Records must stay retrievable for 5 years under 7 CFR 205.103(b)(4), no matter which tool you used to create them. Trazo imports COG Pro CSV exports white-glove — reach out and we'll walk your records in with you.
education.detail.renewalSeason.occspDesc: USDA's Organic Certification Cost Share Program (OCCSP), run by your county Farm Service Agency office or a participating state agency, takes applications for the 2025 and 2026 program years until December 31, 2026. It reimburses up to 75% of eligible certification costs, up to $750 per certification scope (crops, wild crops, livestock, processing/handling, state organic program fees). Eligible costs are the fees of USDA organic certification itself; recordkeeping software, Trazo included, is not on FSA's list. Funds are paid first come, first served (FSA announcement, July 2, 2026).
education.detail.renewalSeason.planRevie: Your renewal starts from last year's plan, and most of its answers carry forward unchanged. Before a plan is filed — and all year on an active plan — Trazo lists what your dated records did after each answer was written: ground you began managing, seasons started and closed, change notices filed, materials added, affidavits, incidents, parcels the plan never names, and modules not revisited in a year. It never reads your prose and never blocks the Submit button — you may well have re-read a section and decided it still holds. It sits under your plan on the screen and prints on the first page of the renewal packet, so the plan you send describes the farm you run.
Before you file: the plan review list
education.detail.renewalSeason.readiness: Your farm home's readiness card and certifier deadlines show which of these pieces are still outstanding, and the packet export assembles the paperwork from records you've already logged.
education.detail.renewalSeason.whyNowDes: October through April is when your records are freshest and your workload is lightest — the natural window to reconcile the season before certifier deadlines arrive.
education.detail.renewalSeason.whyNowTit: Why postharvest is the right time
education.detail.renewalSeason.windowCco: CCOF: renewal packages arrive in early November (November 3 in 2025), due January 1
education.detail.renewalSeason.windowOtc: Oregon Tilth (OTCO): due January 1 or April 1, whichever date Tilth assigns your operation
education.detail.renewalSeason.windowWsd: WSDA (Washington State Dept. of Agriculture) — due March 1
education.detail.scoreOptimization.bench: Photograph your essential activities — planting, harvest and anything you apply — and log the rest as it happens. What matters is that every practice you performed has a record and every record has a date, not that the season hits a target count.
education.detail.scoreOptimization.certD: Paperwork: certification, inspections and compliance — the third-party documents
education.detail.scoreOptimization.goalD: A complete season record means fewer gaps for your certifier's reviewer to query, less to reconstruct at audit time, and more for a buyer to check. This guide shows what complete looks like, category by category.
education.detail.scoreOptimization.goalT: Goal: A Season With No Gaps
education.detail.scoreOptimization.growi: In the field: planting, irrigation, field work and harvest — the core of your season
education.detail.scoreOptimization.mista: Missing photos on essential activities: planting, harvest and input applications are where an inspector most wants visual evidence
Empty core activities: a season with no field work or no input applications has holes a reviewer will always ask about
Batch documentation weeks later: photos taken at the time of the work are credible evidence — a reconstruction from memory is exactly what an inspector probes
Photographing everything equally: put your photo effort into essential activities first; irrigation and weather notes don't need photos at all
Leaving out the paperwork: certificates, inspections and audits belong in the record — they are the third-party documents reviewers ask for first
education.detail.scoreOptimization.mustH: Planting and harvest — the two ends of the trace from a sold lot back to the ground
Every input application, with the product named as it appears on the label
Soil and amendment work: compost, manure, cover crops, soil tests
Pest and scouting rounds — including the ones where you found nothing
Certification and compliance paperwork: inspections, certificates, correspondence
The Records a Reviewer Expects to Find
education.detail.scoreOptimization.pestD: Pest and scouting: what you found, what you released, what you did
education.detail.scoreOptimization.photo: Always photograph: planting, harvest, chemical labels
When practical: pruning, soil tests, scouting
Skip guilt-free: irrigation, weather, general notes
Input applications: photograph the label and the application (up to 5 photos per record)
At least 1 photo on essential activities gives the reviewer evidence instead of just an entry
education.detail.scoreOptimization.soilD: Soil and amendments: soil tests, compost, cover crops
education.detail.scoreOptimization.treat: What you applied: input applications and soil amendments — the records reviewers scrutinize most closely
education.detail.scoreOptimization.treeF: Tree & Nut Crops (Walnuts, Almonds, Citrus, Avocados)
education.detail.scoreOptimization.weath: Weather and other: the context that explains a decision or a yield
education.detail.seasonLifecycle.afterDe: A finished season is a closed record, not a dead one. Work dated after the finish date — a shipment out of storage, winter cover going in, post-harvest field work — logs as a normal activity with its own later date, and it belongs to the same lot's trail. What a finished season refuses is a new record dated inside the closed window: that goes in as a correction on the record it belongs to, with a reason. You can still file a correction on any activity, and if you kept the lot private at finish you can still publish it later from the Buyer Page. Corrections appear in your packet under Documented Corrections, with your reason attached — which is exactly what a certifier wants to see.
education.detail.seasonLifecycle.finishD: Finishing writes the lot header: harvest amount, unit, lot number, finish date, quality grade and harvest method. Trazo offers the amount by adding up your harvest records — picks only, so buffer-row fruit stays out and a post-harvest or transport record repeating the same quantity is not counted twice. Check the figure against your weigh tickets before you confirm.
education.detail.seasonLifecycle.finishW: Finishing does not undo. The lot header is the number your sales are reconciled against and the first thing a certifier reads, and it freezes here. The activity records freeze with it — from that point they take corrections with a reason, not ordinary edits.
Read the header before you confirm
education.detail.seasonLifecycle.introDe: An inspector does not review your farm year in the abstract. They pick a lot you sold and trace it backward: to the field it grew on, the inputs that touched it, and the harvest that produced it. In Trazo that trace is a season: one crop, on one parcel, for one cycle. Everything you log hangs off it, and everything the packet prints about that lot comes from it.
education.detail.seasonLifecycle.introTi: A season is the unit your certifier audits
education.detail.seasonLifecycle.log1: “Log this” on a plan item opens the activity form with the type already chosen. You supply the date, the amounts and the details. Save, and that plan item closes as logged and links to the record you just wrote.
education.detail.seasonLifecycle.log2: “Not this season” takes a practice off the checklist and asks why. The reason is kept — for an inspector, a practice considered and set aside with a reason reads far better than a blank.
education.detail.seasonLifecycle.log3: An activity you add directly is a full record, but it does not close a plan item. The plan is your checklist, not a mirror of your log; tidy it when it suits you.
education.detail.seasonLifecycle.log4: Amounts, product names, application methods and photos belong on the record, never on the plan. The record is what the inspector reads.
education.detail.seasonLifecycle.logTitl: 3. Log the work as you do it
education.detail.seasonLifecycle.plan1: Nothing on the checklist is a record. A plan item says a practice is expected; the record is what you write afterward, with the date it actually happened.
education.detail.seasonLifecycle.plan2: Every suggestion arrives unticked. You decide which ones belong on your farm.
education.detail.seasonLifecycle.plan3: On an organic season, materials prohibited under § 205.105 are still listed so you can see they were considered — but they cannot be ticked.
education.detail.seasonLifecycle.plan4: You can set any practice aside with a reason and put it back later, right up until the season is finished or published. What you cannot do is invent a plan item out of nothing — the checklist comes from the template, and the work you do outside it is recorded as an activity.
education.detail.seasonLifecycle.planDes: Picking a crop template writes you a season checklist: the practices that crop usually needs, each carrying an agronomic window — “December - February”, “Throughout season”, “70-80 days after planting”. Windows, never dates.
education.detail.seasonLifecycle.startDe: Start a season from the parcel it will grow on. You give it the crop, the start date, the production method and the harvest window you expect. From then on the parcel shows a season underway, and every activity you add knows which season it belongs to.
education.detail.seasonLifecycle.startNo: A parcel can carry more than one open season at a time: a perennial planting running a 2025 and a 2026 cycle, or ground you double-crop. Finishing closes the season you opened it from, so read the crop and the dates on the finish page before you confirm. Closing is irreversible, and closing the wrong season cannot be taken back.
education.detail.seasonLifecycle.whereDe: Farm → parcel → the season card. The plan sits on the season page beside the activity timeline. Finish season is on the season page, and on the parcel page once the season has at least one activity logged.
education.detail.traceback.callsTitle: Calls that do not start with an invoice
education.detail.traceback.certifierDesc: If you share a review link, your certifier can run the same trace from it without an account. It covers only that farm's sales inside the link's period, every trace shows in your link activity, and a file opens only if you chose to share your source files. Missing links are shown to them as facts, with no fix buttons.
education.detail.traceback.closedNote: A finished season is locked. To change a record in it, use a correction, which keeps the original and the change side by side for your certifier.
education.detail.traceback.gapInput: no supplier, invoice number or lot number. Open the record and add what the purchase invoice and the label say.
education.detail.traceback.gapPick: no lot code, so nothing on a bin or an invoice can point to it. Add the code written on its bins or tags.
education.detail.traceback.gapReceipt: "Fix it here" opens Documents already filed to that record, as its purchase receipt. Choose the file and confirm. Filed that way it counts as the record's receipt everywhere: on the trace, on the record, in the audit export and in your packet's receipts folder. A lab report or a photo filed on the same record stays an attachment.
education.detail.traceback.gapSale: no invoice or bill of lading number, no file of the paper behind it, or no harvest pick named. A saved sale cannot be edited, so a missing number or pick means voiding the sale and entering it again; the file is attached from the sale's row in the season.
education.detail.traceback.gapSeason: no lot ID, so a container tag cannot name it. You enter it when you finish the season.
education.detail.traceback.gapsIntro: Each link the records do not carry is named where it breaks, with a "Fix it here" button that takes you to the right place and back to the trace when you save.
education.detail.traceback.habitDesc: A few weeks before your inspection, trace one random recent sale and one sale from a document in your files, and fix what they show. Those are the two ways an inspector usually starts.
education.detail.traceback.introDesc: At inspection, the inspector picks a sale off an invoice or bill of lading and walks it back: which harvest pick it came from, which field and season, and every input applied there, with the supplier, invoice and lot behind each one. 7 CFR 205.103(b)(2) asks that your records disclose every activity and transaction in enough detail to be readily understood and audited. Trazo runs that same walk on your records, so you see where it breaks before they do.
education.detail.traceback.introTitle: This is the walk your inspector takes
education.detail.traceback.limitDesc: It shows what your records connect and names what they do not. It does not grade your records, send anything to anyone, or replace your certifier's review.
education.detail.traceback.limitTitle: What a trace does not do
education.detail.traceback.packer: They quote their own receipt or weigh-ticket number. If you recorded it on the harvest pick, typing it opens the sale that pick went into.
education.detail.traceback.recall: Type the lot or invoice number of the compost, spray or seed. Trazo lists the sales of each season it was applied in, with who bought how much. The screen lists 20 sales at most and says so when there are more; the rest are in each season's sales records.
education.detail.traceback.residue: Each spray shows how many days before the next pick on the same section it went on, beside the pre-harvest interval you recorded for it, and is marked when the pick came sooner. That is arithmetic on your own dates, not a judgement about the label: check the label and your records before you answer.
education.detail.traceback.residueLabel: A buyer asks about a residue.
education.detail.traceback.step1: From Documents, choose "Trace a sale". From a season's sales, choose "Trace this sale" on the row you want.
education.detail.traceback.step2: Type what is printed on a document: the invoice, the bill of lading, the lot code on the bins, the packer's receipt number, or the lot or invoice of something you applied. Or choose "Random recent sale", which is how an inspector often picks one.
education.detail.traceback.step3: Lot codes and invoice numbers can repeat across seasons. When more than one sale matches, Trazo lists them and you choose the one on the document; it never picks for you.
education.detail.traceback.step4: The sale, the picks it names, the season and field, every input applied that season, and what you harvested against what you sold. Files you attached open from the trace.

tooltip.blockchainRecorded.example: Example: the certifier packet's integrity line lets a reviewer confirm the file matches what was finished
tooltip.blockchainRecorded.explanation: When a production is finished, Trazo computes a digital fingerprint of the documented records. It appears as an integrity line in the certifier packet so a reviewer can confirm the file was not altered after finishing. It proves the data was not changed — it does not verify farming practices, and it is not shown to shoppers.
tooltip.carbonFootprint.example: Covers farmer-controlled emissions: fuel combustion, fertilizer application, and equipment operation
tooltip.carbonFootprint.explanation: The total amount of greenhouse gases produced by direct farming operations — fuel, fertilizer, equipment, and irrigation. Think of it as the environmental “receipt” for growing your food.
tooltip.carbonScore.example: Example: diesel use and fertilizer applications each contribute a calculated amount
tooltip.co2e.example: 1 ton CO₂e = driving 2,400 miles in an average car
tooltip.co2e.explanation: A standard unit that combines all greenhouse gases (CO₂, methane, nitrous oxide) into a single measurement. Like converting different currencies into dollars for easy comparison.
tooltip.conservationTillage.example: No-till farming can store 1.2 tons of CO₂ per hectare annually
tooltip.conservationTillage.explanation: Farming methods that disturb soil as little as possible, keeping plant residue on the surface to protect soil and store carbon.
tooltip.emissionFactors.example: EPA provides exact CO₂ amounts for tractors, fertilizers, and other farm inputs
tooltip.emissionFactors.explanation: Published research data that shows how much greenhouse gas different farming activities produce. These are the scientific “recipes” used to calculate carbon footprints accurately.
tooltip.fertilizationEvent.example: NPK 10-10-10 applied at 100 kg/hectare = detailed transparency record
tooltip.fertilizationEvent.explanation: Document NPK applications, organic amendments, and soil nutrients. Includes concentration validation to ensure accurate carbon calculations and consumer transparency.
tooltip.fungicideEvent.example: Preventive applications typically use less product than curative
tooltip.fungicideEvent.explanation: Document disease prevention and treatment including copper, sulfur, and synthetic fungicides. Shows consumers your plant health management practices.
tooltip.harvestEvent.example: Recording yield data enables transparency benchmarking
tooltip.harvestEvent.explanation: Document crop collection including yield quantity, equipment used, and transportation. Consumers see your quality selection and handling practices.
tooltip.herbicideEvent.example: Example: an herbicide application logged with the product, rate, target weeds and area treated
tooltip.herbicideEvent.explanation: Record weed management activities including pre-emergent and post-emergent applications. Document organic alternatives and cover crop termination.
tooltip.irrigationEvent.example: Drip irrigation uses 25-50% less water than flood methods
tooltip.irrigationEvent.explanation: Record water management practices including volume, method (drip, sprinkler, flood), and duration. Shows consumers your water stewardship and resource efficiency.
tooltip.pestControlEvent.example: IPM practices can reduce pesticide use by 40%
tooltip.pestControlEvent.explanation: Document pest management including IPM practices, pesticide applications, and beneficial insect releases. Consumers value transparency about crop protection methods.
tooltip.photoDocumentation.example: 86% means 19 out of 22 events have photo evidence attached
tooltip.photoDocumentation.explanation: The percentage of farming events that include photo evidence. Photos provide visual proof of farming practices — consumers can see exactly how their food was grown.
tooltip.plantingEvent.example: Example: recording certified seed varieties gives your reviewer the § 205.204 answer up front
tooltip.plantingEvent.explanation: Record crop planting including seed variety, planting density, and soil preparation. Shows consumers the start of your growing journey.
tooltip.precisionAgriculture.example: Like having a smart phone for farming - everything is measured and optimized
tooltip.precisionAgriculture.explanation: Farming technology that uses GPS, sensors, and data to apply exactly the right amount of inputs (water, fertilizer) in exactly the right places, reducing waste.
tooltip.pruningEvent.example: Proper pruning improves yield quality and reduces disease
tooltip.pruningEvent.explanation: Record plant maintenance including seasonal pruning, thinning, and training. Includes fuel consumption for powered equipment to track environmental impact.
tooltip.quickAdd.example: Example: logging 5-7 events weekly keeps the season's record complete as it happens
tooltip.quickAdd.explanation: The fastest way to log farming activities in under 60 seconds. Choose from 7 event types, smart defaults pre-fill common values, and voice capture lets you document hands-free.
tooltip.sustainabilityImpact.example: High impact = actively helping the environment, not just avoiding harm
tooltip.sustainabilityImpact.explanation: How this farming practice affects the environment - including soil health, water quality, biodiversity, and climate.
tooltip.usdaFactorsUsed.example: Government-published data ensures consistent, reliable carbon calculations
tooltip.usdaFactorsUsed.explanation: Carbon calculations for this event use official emission factors published by the EPA and USDA. This ensures consistent methodology across all farms — not a verification of farming practices themselves.
tour.activities.step1.content: Start here after work in the field — spraying, irrigation, harvest, an input purchase. Pick what you did and the form opens with the right fields.
tour.activities.step1.title: Log an activity
tour.activities.step2.content: The calendar is the month view you can hand to your certifier; the list is for searching and filtering. Same records, two views.
tour.activities.step2.title: Calendar or list
tour.activities.step3.content: Every activity lands here, and the same entry feeds your Organic System Plan, your certifier packet and your buyer page. One entry, two outputs.
tour.activities.step3.title: Your season in one place
tour.buyer.step1.content: Scans all-time and in the last 30 days, how many seasons are published, and how many document requests are waiting on you.
tour.buyer.step1.title: What buyers are seeing
tour.buyer.step2.content: A season stays off the public page until you switch Public on, which needs the season finished first. Preview it and download its QR code and lot tags from the same row. A private buyer review link can share in-progress seasons without publishing anything.
tour.buyer.step2.title: Publish a season
tour.buyer.step3.content: When a buyer asks for a certificate or a record, the request arrives here. Open ones are counted on the card above.
tour.buyer.step3.title: Document requests
tour.checklist.pilot.howSetupWorks.send: Send your existing records to Oscar:
tour.checklist.pilot.howSetupWorks.enter: Oscar enters them in Trazo under his own login.
tour.checklist.pilot.howSetupWorks.check: You check them before anything is filed.
tour.checklist.pilot.operatorSetup: You are setting up this farm for the grower
tour.checklist.pilot.operatorSetup.body: Records you enter show your name.
tour.checklist.pilot.operatorSetup.check: Only the grower can sign the annual update or mark the plan as submitted.
tour.checklist.pilot.ofpp: A fraud prevention plan is on file in Trazo
tour.checklist.pilot.osp: The Organic System Plan in Trazo has text in all six § 205.201(a) sections, or has been submitted
tour.checklist.pilot.parcel: A parcel is on file in Trazo
tour.checklist.pilot.records: Season records are on file in Trazo
tour.checklist.setupHelpPrompt: Have last season's records somewhere else?
tour.checklist.title: Getting Started
tour.checklist.writer.item1: Add a parcel to your farm
tour.documents.step1.content: Certificates, input labels, lab results, signed contracts — anything your certifier may ask to see, kept where you can find it.
tour.documents.step1.title: Upload a document
tour.documents.step2.content: Filter by folder. The number on each chip is how many rows that folder will show, so you can see what is missing without opening it.
tour.documents.step2.title: Folders and counts
tour.documents.step3.content: Regenerate an export and the older copies fold into one row as versions, newest on top. Files you upload yourself always keep their own row.
tour.documents.step3.title: One row per document
tour.farmProfile.step1.content: Add your organic certifications here. A USDA Organic certificate is cross-checked against the USDA Organic Integrity Database, and your certifier and certificate number appear on your public product pages.
tour.farmProfile.step1.title: Add your certifications
tour.farmProfile.step2.content: Upload your Organic Fraud Prevention Plan and name the person responsible. Required since March 2024 for certified organic operations — your audit export reports it as a gap until it is on file.
tour.farmProfile.step2.title: Fraud prevention plan
tour.milestone.firstEvent.bodyEarly: Keep going. Every activity you record now is one less thing to reconstruct at renewal.
tour.milestone.firstEvent.bodyLate: Each entry adds to the record you hand your certifier.
tour.milestone.firstFinish.bodyEarly: This season's records are complete. Publish it and buyers can scan the QR code to see how it was grown.
tour.milestone.firstFinish.bodyLate: Publish it to make the season visible to your buyers.
tour.osp.step1.content: The version you are working on and how many modules are answered. Once a plan is submitted it becomes read-only — start a new version to change it.
tour.osp.step1.title: Your plan, version by version
tour.osp.step2.content: Each card is one part of the Organic System Plan. The badged card is the next one to work on — Trazo picks the first module that is neither finished nor marked not applicable.
tour.osp.step2.title: Farm-wide modules
tour.osp.step3.content: Each field needs its own application too: land history, buffers, adjoining land use. Parcels with work outstanding are listed first.
tour.osp.step3.title: Parcel applications
tour.osp.step4.content: Exports the plan and its answers as one PDF to send your certifier. Your certifying agent decides what they accept.
tour.osp.step4.title: Download the packet
tour.parcel.step1.content: See your current season's crop, start date and status at a glance.
tour.parcel.step1.title: Current season
tour.parcel.step2.content: Every activity you document appears here. The same records feed your OSP, your audit dossier and your buyer page.
tour.parcel.step2.title: Activities
tour.parcel.step3.content: Tap Log activity and pick what you did (planting, irrigation, harvest). The form opens with voice and template shortcuts ready.
tour.parcel.step3.title: Log activity
tour.parcel.step4.content: Every past and current season on this parcel, with its records and status.
tour.parcel.step4.title: Seasons
tour.production.step1.content: Pick the crop for this season. Each one brings a list of the practices it usually needs, with their typical windows.
tour.production.step1.title: Choose your crop
tour.production.step2.content: Tick the practices you expect to carry out. Nothing is recorded yet — each one becomes a to-do you log, with the real date, when you actually do it.
tour.production.step2.title: Your season plan
tour.welcomeFresh.step1.content: Everything you record (activities, plans, documents) belongs to the farm named here. If you manage more than one farm, switch from the sidebar.
tour.welcomeFresh.step1.title: Your farm
tour.welcomeFresh.step2.content: The readiness checks still open on this farm — plan on file, fraud prevention plan, records for the season. Each one says what is not on file in Trazo yet and where to add it.
tour.welcomeFresh.step2.title: Before your certifier packet
tour.welcomeFresh.step3.content: Parcels are your fields or blocks. Add one so you have somewhere to record activities and start a season.
tour.welcomeFresh.step3.title: Add your first parcel
tour.welcomeFresh.step4.content: Activities is your day-to-day log. Organic System Plan builds your OSP, Documents holds your certificates and exports, and the Buyer Page is what you share outside the farm.
tour.welcomeFresh.step4.title: Where everything lives
tour.welcomeInvited.step1.content: This is the farm you are working on. Switch to another of your team's farms from the sidebar.
tour.welcomeInvited.step1.title: Your team's farm
tour.welcomeInvited.step2.content: The readiness checks still open on this farm. It is the fastest read of what is left to do before renewal.
tour.welcomeInvited.step2.title: Before the certifier packet
tour.welcomeInvited.step3.content: Each parcel is a field or block. Open one to see its seasons and everything recorded against it.
tour.welcomeInvited.step3.title: Farm parcels
tour.welcomeInvited.step4.content: Log activities, answer Organic System Plan modules, file documents and check what buyers can see — all from the sidebar.
tour.welcomeInvited.step4.title: Navigate and contribute
tour.welcomeViewer.step1.content: This is the farm you are reading. Its seasons and parcels are further down; your team's other farms are in the sidebar.
tour.welcomeViewer.step1.title: Farm overview
tour.welcomeViewer.step2.content: The readiness checks still open on this farm before its certifier packet.
tour.welcomeViewer.step2.title: Renewal readiness
tour.welcomeViewer.step3.content: Each parcel is a field or block. Open one to read its seasons and the activities recorded against them.
tour.welcomeViewer.step3.title: Farm parcels
tour.welcomeViewer.step4.content: Activities, the Organic System Plan, Documents and the Buyer Page are all in the sidebar. You can read everything; the farm's admins make the changes.
tour.welcomeViewer.step4.title: Explore
